t: Chaucer set a collection of tales inside a pilgrimage, a framework no earlier work is known to have used, and let the pilgrims' classes, occupations and views shape the stories they tell.
He planned about 120 stories, four from each of some 30 pilgrims, but most scholars think the work was incomplete at the end of his life, and there is no consensus on its intended order.
No manuscript in Chaucer's hand survives; the text comes from 84 manuscripts and four incunabula, and later writers added tales and prologues to fill its gaps.
dyk: The Canterbury Tales survives in more manuscripts than any other vernacular English literary text except Prick of Conscience, yet Derek Pearsall cautions that this should not be taken as proof of its popularity in the century after Chaucer's death.
ev: Chaucer begins writing The Canterbury Tales, a work he continues until 1400
The period of composition ends with the Tales incomplete, as most scholars think
John Lydgate writes The Siege of Thebes, which places himself among the pilgrims
William Caxton prints the first edition of the Tales
John Stow prints Lydgate's Siege of Thebes
John Urry's edition prints the Tale of Beryn alongside the Tales
F. J. Furnivall identifies nine Groups of tales under the auspices of the Chaucer Society
Following John M. Manly and Edith Rickert, scholars increasingly favour the Hengwrt manuscript over Ellesmere

f.made: Geoffrey Chaucer, who wrote it between 1387 and 1400 while serving as Controller of Customs, Justice of the Peace and Clerk of the King's Works; copied by scribes, among them one identified as Adam Pinkhurst
f.form: An anthology of twenty-four tales in Middle English, mostly in verse with five stressed syllables to the line, set within a frame tale of pilgrims; Sir Thopas and the prose tales differ in metre, and four tales use rhyme royal
f.where: No manuscript in Chaucer's own hand survives; 84 manuscripts and four incunabula editions are known, including William Caxton's 1476 edition, of which ten copies survive, among them one at the British Library and one at the Folger Shakespeare Library
f.known: The General Prologue's portraits of the pilgrims; the storytelling contest; the Knight's Tale and the Miller's interruption; the Pardoner and the Summoner; the Wife of Bath; the pilgrimage to Saint Thomas Becket's shrine; the Middle English of a London dialect; its incompleteness
